items.title: HY advance-decline line still sucks — equities are the lagging leg
items.idea: @vixologist's update on the high-yield A/D line: breadth inside HY credit is still deteriorating, and his read is that equities 'can't be surprised' if they get worse. Credit breadth is rolling over while the index level sits only marginally below September highs.
items.angle: Pairs with the CDS blowout in the Market Ear note: the credit tape is leading, equity is catching down. Watch HY A/D as the tell for whether the tech selloff is contained.
items.tweetA: HY breadth is a lead indicator and nobody has it on a screen. The index looks fine because 10 names carry it; the A/D line says the other 90% of issuers are already repricing. Equities are the last to know.
items.tweetB: If you wanted a reason the oil collapse and lower yields didn't rescue Nasdaq on Monday, start here. Credit never confirmed the bounce.

charts.desc: HY A/D line trending down while index holds up. Divergence chart.

items.title: Goldman Risk Appetite Indicator opened the week >2 SD below average
items.idea: Robbie Stankard (GS): the Risk Appetite Indicator entered the week more than 2 standard deviations below its mean. That is a washout reading on the positioning side, before Monday's further Nasdaq and SOX losses.
items.angle: Market Ear separately says the contrarian buy zone only starts below -1 on its scale and history after big RAI drops is a coin flip. Washout is necessary, not sufficient.
items.tweetA: RAI >2 SD below average, and then Monday sold off anyway. The positioning reset doesn't mark the low, it marks the point where forced sellers are the only sellers left. Different problem.
items.tweetB: Everyone is asking 'is it capitulation'. Capitulation needs a catalyst that flips flow. Election night is the only one on the calendar, and it can't fix AI financing.

charts.desc: GS RAI z-score line, deep below mean.

items.title: Inverted call skew collapses: 44% of S&P top 100 in early Oct → 10% now
items.idea: Cboe's Mandy Xu: the share of top-100 S&P names trading with inverted call skew (a marker of extreme bullish sentiment, calls richer than puts) fell from 44% in early October to 10%. Euphoric upside chasing has been cleaned out in four weeks.
items.angle: Speculative upside convexity is gone. That removes the gamma squeeze fuel that powered the October highs and the tech 'melt-up' narrative.
items.tweetA: 44% to 10% in four weeks. Calls went from being bid like lottery tickets to being offered. That's what a sentiment regime change looks like in options, and it happened before the headline selloff finished.
items.tweetB: The crowd that was paying up for upside in early Oct is now the crowd paying up for downside. Same people, same names. Positioning is a rental, not a view.

charts.desc: % of top-100 S&P names with inverted call skew, peak 44% to 10%.

items.title: Trend breadth reverses: % of S&P stocks with 50d > 200d rolling over
items.idea: Willie Delwiche (Hi Mount): the share of stocks whose 50-day average is above their 200-day has begun to recede meaningfully, reversing and more the improvement earlier in the year. Index-level uptrend is 'holding on for dear life' while the internal trend count erodes.
items.angle: Internal trend erosion + index near highs = classic late-cycle divergence. Combine with Lord Fed's '406 stocks green, index red' day for a breadth-has-decoupled narrative.
items.tweetA: The index is a cap-weighted opinion. The 50/200 count is a vote. The vote just flipped.
items.tweetB: S&P down a few percent from September, but the share of stocks in uptrends has erased the entire 2026 improvement. Index drawdowns that look shallow with deep internals tend to resolve one way.

charts.desc: % of SPX members with 50d MA above 200d, falling back.

items.title: Safe is expensive: Low Vol at ~19x, Dividend Yield factor 90th pctl; Growth 40th, Momentum 30th
items.idea: GS (Brian Garrett via @blakemillardcfa): S&P 500 Low Vol index trades ~19x, near the year's highs. Dividend Yield factor sits in the 90th percentile of valuation, Valuation factor 80th; Growth is now 40th and Momentum 30th percentile. The defensive trade is crowded and the growth/momentum trade is cheapening.
items.angle: Rotation into safety has already happened; the pain trade may be that Growth and Momentum are the cheap leg. Counter to the 'tech is broken' consensus.
items.tweetA: Low vol at 19x. You are paying growth multiples for utilities-like cash flows because everyone wants to hide in the same room. Momentum at the 30th percentile. Someone is going to look very smart or very late.
items.tweetB: Which is the crowded trade: owning cheapened Growth that just broke its 200dma, or owning expensive defensives that everyone ran into? Valuation says the first. Flow says the second.

charts.desc: Factor valuation percentiles: Low Vol/Yield high, Growth/Momentum low.

items.title: DOJ asked SCOTUS to segregate ballots tied to 20,000+ California voters — Court said no
items.idea: On the eve of Election Day the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to segregate ballots associated with 20,000+ California voters based on an unverified list; the justices rejected it the same day. Two lower courts (district judge Oct 28, 9th Circuit Oct 30) had already rejected the evidence, with the judge saying the remedy would 'wreak havoc' on election administration.
items.angle: Election-process litigation risk didn't produce an order; the next catalyst is the first post-election filing. Relevant to how much weight to put on 'contested outcome' tail scenarios.
items.tweetA: 20,000 names, no verification, three courts, zero relief. The legal tail on election night just got thinner. The market is still pricing political uncertainty as if it hasn't.
items.tweetB: Ballots can't be un-commingled after counting. That's the whole case for segregation, and also why courts won't order it on an unverified list. Watch the first post-election filing for voter-level verification, not rhetoric.

items.title: Cyberattack raised fridge temperatures at dozens of Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt stores
items.idea: In the 'Things happen' section: an attack on dozens of Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt stores in Europe raised refrigerator temperatures, following a similar incident in France last month. The target is refrigeration control, not payment or data.
items.angle: Cyber moving from data theft to physical spoilage of inventory. Food retail OT security, insurers, and ransomware pricing.
items.tweetA: Fridge temperature setpoints are now an attack surface. Not data, not payments. Spoiled inventory. Second incident in two months across European grocers. Somebody is testing how much downtime a grocer can tolerate.
items.tweetB: Everyone prices cyber as a data-breach risk. A cold chain attack is a P&L event with a clock on it: hours until product is lost. That's insurance repricing material.

items.title: Judge dismisses Harvard admissions-records suit; FBI/Hunter Biden laptop case thrown out
items.idea: Two dismissals in a day: the administration's lawsuit seeking Harvard admissions data over race-consideration was dismissed, and charges against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the Hunter Biden laptop were tossed.
items.angle: Courts continue to be a binding constraint on executive action pre-midterms. Policy-risk base rate for litigation-driven agendas.
items.tweetA: Three courtroom losses for the administration in a week on election-adjacent matters (ballots, Harvard, FBI case). Courts are the real policy-risk governor right now, not Congress.
items.tweetB: Higher ed endowments trade on the premise that federal pressure is litigable. Today's ruling supports that.

items.title: ING adds travel eSIMs inside bank app via Gigs
items.idea: ING partnered with embedded-mobile provider Gigs to sell global travel data eSIMs in the banking app. A bank distributing a telecom product as a feature.
items.angle: Embedded-telecom as a bank retention/interchange play. Gigs is the infra layer.
items.tweetA: A bank sells eSIMs. Telcos lose the travel-roaming margin to a bank app, not to another telco. Embedded finance's mirror image: embedded telecom.
items.tweetB: Roaming was the highest-margin consumer telecom line. ING plus Gigs is the unbundling.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: The AI financing feedback loop: falling equity raises the cost of capex funding
items.idea: Innes: phase one of AI was funded from hyperscaler cash flow and rising equity. Now falling equity raises the effective cost of capital, pushing the buildout onto bond markets just as investors ask for proof of returns. 'Debt markets are asked to carry more of the load' as the cheaper equity currency makes bond access more important.
items.angle: Direct bridge to CDS records (Market Ear) and META FCF -$2.1B (Lord Fed). Financing the next cheque is the story, not demand.
items.tweetA: Equity is the cheapest capital until it isn't. When the stock falls, the capex has to go to the bond market. That's how you turn a growth story into a credit story without anyone announcing it.
items.tweetB: Meta: $32.8B operating cash, $34.9B capex. Oracle back for another $10B bonds. Add falling equity and CDS at records. Capex is now funded at the margin by whoever will lend at that price.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Nasdaq 100 into correction even after oil -7%, easier yields, softer dollar
items.idea: Monday: Crude -7%, long yields eased, dollar softened, Washington talked down Iran escalation — and Nasdaq faded from +1.2% at the open to break Friday's lows, entering correction territory. Innes: 'when a market refuses the cure, the diagnosis usually matters more than the medicine.'
items.angle: A macro-relief day that failed is information: the sell-off driver is no longer rates/oil but AI funding. Trade the driver, not the macro.
items.tweetA: Oil -7%. Yields lower. Dollar softer. Nasdaq down. When every macro tailwind gets handed to you and the index still sells, the macro wasn't the problem.
items.tweetB: Rates-down-equities-down is the signature of a growth scare plus a funding scare. Duration isn't saving you if the cash flows are the question.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Brent -7.63% to $104.77 on Iran peace-talk headlines; war premium 'evaporated'
items.idea: Brent fell 7.63% to $104.77, WTI -7.36% to $96.46 after Iran's President said the government was authorized to pursue peace talks, Qatari mediators went to Tehran and Trump said a deal 'could happen.' Innes argues fair value was low-to-mid $90s with Gulf exports back near prewar levels — the premium was insurance against post-midterm strikes.
items.angle: Event-risk premium of ~$10+ priced out on headlines alone. Compare with Market Ear: trend followers entered long energy, so unwind risk is mechanical.
items.tweetA: $10 of oil was a hedge against a date: the midterms. When the narrative flips from 'strikes after the election' to 'talks', the hedge has nothing under it. And CTAs were long into it.
items.tweetB: If balance says $90s and spot is $104, the market was paying $10 for an option on escalation. Now it's cheap to buy that option again, if you think talks fail.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Apple beat and guided above consensus, still -4% after hours
items.idea: Apple revenue +12% to $114.5B, iPhone strong, Mac beat, holiday guide above consensus — shares fell ~4% after hours. China missed by >$1B, iPad disappointed, wearables -8%. Apple had added ~$1T in market cap since late June as the 'safe house' of megacap tech.
items.angle: When the safe house gets sold on a beat-and-raise the hurdle rate is brutal. Links to GS stat that EPS beats in TMT are rewarded -0.76% next day.
items.tweetA: Up $1T since June, then sold on a beat-and-raise. The hurdle rate for megacap tech is now 'perfect'. Apple was the last place to hide.
items.tweetB: GS: beats outside TMT outperform by +1.72% next day, inside TMT -0.76%. Apple just joined the TMT bucket.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: SOX -12% in three sessions; first close below 200dma since June 2025
items.idea: SOX lost another 3.4% Monday after -7.2% Friday, ~12% in three sessions, and failed to regain its 200-day after closing below it Friday for the first time since June 2025. Innes: once suppliers lose technical support as financing needs grow, the market asks who gets paid back. (Market Ear dates the prior break to May 2025.)
items.angle: Chip suppliers are the first link in the chain that gets repriced when capex financing becomes the question.
items.tweetA: SOX -7.2%, then -3.4%. When the shovel-sellers break their 200dma, the market starts asking who is paying for the shovels.
items.tweetB: Semis fwd P/E at 16x (Market Ear) after a 12% drop in three days. The multiple is cheap. The funding question isn't.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: PBOC to encourage greater use of stock-support tools
items.idea: PBOC said it will encourage more use of stock-support tools and improve their terms, giving mainland and HK equities a policy cushion while Japan/Korea absorb the semis hit. Innes: the first pop isn't the test, the close is.
items.angle: China decoupling from the US tech correction in session flow. Policy put vs conviction.
items.tweetA: PBOC offering an equity put while US tech breaks the 200dma. First signal whether Asia trades as one risk block or separates.
items.tweetB: A price-insensitive buyer can absorb selling. It can't fix earnings or consumption. Same test as every prior stock-support episode.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Midterms: relief rally if Senate holds and AI-regulation fears prove overdone
items.idea: History favors a post-election rally and desks argue the expected Democratic gain is priced. A Republican Senate hold could trigger relief, 'particularly if fears of tougher AI regulation prove overdone.' Innes: the election removes political uncertainty but cannot fix AI financing or the semis' technical damage.
items.angle: AI regulation is a named risk factor in the equity narrative into the vote. Election night is a catalyst for the political leg only.
items.tweetA: Market is treating Tuesday as a clearing event. It clears the political premium, not the funding problem. Two risks, one catalyst.
items.tweetB: AI regulation as a named risk into the vote. If Democrats take the House, which bills move first? That's the real trade, not the headline seat count.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Oracle back in bond market for another $10B days after new AI infra plans
items.idea: Innes cites Oracle seeking another $10B in bonds only days after laying out fresh AI infrastructure plans, alongside Anthropic outlining spending 'more at home in a sovereign infrastructure budget.' The funding burden is migrating to corporate balance sheets.
items.angle: Issuance calendar as an AI-capex stress gauge. Pair with record AI CDS.
items.tweetA: Oracle came back for another $10B within days. The AI buildout is now funded issue by issue, and the spread is the report card.
items.tweetB: Anthropic's spending plans sized like a sovereign budget plus Oracle's serial issuance. At some point the question is who owns this paper.

items.title: NDX closes below 200dma for first time since March; RSI most oversold since July
items.idea: Nasdaq 100 closed below its 200-day for the first time since March; RSI hit its most oversold since July and is approaching March panic extremes. A major trend line sits right around these levels.
items.angle: Technical + oversold + trendline confluence: potential reflex-bounce zone, but credit not confirming.
items.tweetA: First 200dma close since March. RSI near March-panic levels. A bounce is likely here. A durable one needs credit to agree.
items.tweetB: Oversold bounces in a funding scare are sold. The tell is whether HY and CDS confirm.

charts.desc: NDX price vs 200dma with RSI panel and trend line.

items.title: 'Holy SmOX': SOX decisively below 200dma, longer-term trend line is last support
items.idea: SOX closed decisively below its 200-day for the first time since May 2025. The longer-term trend line is the last major support; momentum 'remains awful.'
items.angle: Semis are the funding-scare epicenter. Trend-line support is the level to watch.
items.tweetA: SOX at the last trend line. If it goes, the argument shifts from correction to regime.
items.tweetB: Semi breakdown + 16x fwd P/E: price fell faster than earnings estimates. The question for the next print is estimates, not multiples.

charts.desc: SOX vs 200dma and long-term trend line.

items.title: Expecting a tech rebound while CDS stays this elevated is naive — AI default swaps at records
items.idea: Market Ear: NDX is doing what elevated major CDS spreads imply. Linked ZeroHedge piece: 'hedge stopped hedging, AI default swaps hit records, Goldman finds credit cracking everywhere.'
items.angle: Credit leading equity. AI-related CDS as the risk gauge for hyperscaler/AI-neocloud funding.
items.tweetA: CDS on AI names at records while the equity only just broke the 200dma. Credit usually moves first. Equity is catching up.
items.tweetB: Default swaps at records, serial bond issuance, equity falling. That's the three-legged stool of a financing regime shift.

charts.desc: NDX vs aggregate major CDS spreads.

items.title: Goldman Risk Appetite: one of its largest monthly declines in October, but not yet contrarian-buy (<-1)
items.idea: GS risk indicator saw one of its largest monthly declines in October. Contrarian buy levels start below -1; not there yet.
items.angle: Risk-appetite washout is incomplete on the GS framework.
items.tweetA: Biggest RAI drop of the cycle and still not at contrarian-buy. Washout isn't over.
items.tweetB: Chartbook says >2 SD below average; Market Ear says not yet at the -1 buy line. Two framings of the same indicator. Pick your threshold carefully.

charts.desc: GS RAI with -1 contrarian buy threshold.

items.title: VIX surge is aggressive while SPX is only marginally below mid-September
items.idea: Market Ear: you don't compare trending and mean-reverting assets over long periods, but VIX's surge over the past few weeks is aggressive given SPX is only marginally below mid-Sept levels.
items.angle: Index calm masks dispersion: stress is concentrated in tech/AI. Implied-vol is pricing sector risk, not index drawdown.
items.tweetA: SPX barely below September, VIX up sharply. The index is a rounding error; the stress is under the hood in a handful of names.
items.tweetB: Vol is being bid for correlation to come. Dispersion is paying while index gets repriced.

items.title: CTA convexity: $164bn downside selling vs $120bn upside buying; thresholds 7,713 / 7,544 / 7,082
items.idea: GS/TME: CTA flows negligible this week but one-month setup is large: up to $164bn of selling in a falling market vs $120bn buying in a rising one. Key SPX thresholds: short-term 7,713, medium-term 7,544 (most important), long-term 7,082.
items.angle: Flow levels for the week. A trigger map for mechanical selling.
items.tweetA: $164B of mechanical selling on the downside against $120B of buying on the upside. Key level is 7,544. Below that, flow is not your friend.
items.tweetB: Convexity cuts both ways. A violent squeeze up is as plausible as a breakdown. Size accordingly.

charts.desc: GS CTA flow ladder by SPX level and TME.

items.title: Tech stress near year's highs while broad equity vol stays far below March panic
items.idea: Tech-specific stress is approaching its highest of the year, yet broader equity vol is far from March panic extremes. Divergence 'increasingly interesting.'
items.angle: Sector-specific stress not yet contagion. If broad vol catches up, that's the regime shift.
items.tweetA: Tech stress near year highs. Broad vol well below March. One of these converges.
items.tweetB: Contagion is the question. Credit leads, broad vol follows.

charts.desc: Tech stress gauge vs broad equity vol.

items.title: After the 11 largest RAI drops since 2005, S&P 1m returns ranged -17% to +7%, 6m -32% to +18%
items.idea: Market Ear: positioning reset is no guarantee of a bottom. Plenty of tail risk both directions.
items.angle: Wide dispersion in outcomes: don't treat washouts as buy signals.
items.tweetA: -17% to +7% over one month after similar washouts. That is not an edge, that is a coin flip with fat tails.
items.tweetB: Everyone says 'positioning is washed out'. Eleven prior instances say the range of outcomes is enormous.

charts.desc: S&P forward returns after the 11 largest GS RAI declines.

items.title: Median S&P company revenue growth: 7.4% → 7.2% → 7.0%; Q4 consensus 6.4%
items.idea: FactSet: median S&P 500 company revenue growth slowed from 7.4% in Q1 to 7.2% in Q2 and 7.0% in Q3, with Q4 expected at 6.4%. Not a collapse, but the direction is 'difficult to spin.'
items.angle: Top-line deceleration under the surface of strong AI earnings.
items.tweetA: Median S&P revenue growth: 7.4, 7.2, 7.0, 6.4e. A glide, not a cliff, but every step is lower and the index multiple is not.
items.tweetB: Aggregate earnings are carried by a few AI names. The median company is slowing, which is why 406 stocks can be green on a red index day.

charts.desc: Median S&P 500 revenue growth by quarter incl. Q4 consensus.

items.title: Tech valuations compress sharply; relative-valuation argument getting 'interesting'
items.idea: Tech multiples have compressed toward levels not seen in some time; ironically just as investors flee. Market Ear links to a 'great rotation trap' piece.
items.angle: Relative valuation versus fundamentals is the debate.
items.tweetA: Everyone is leaving tech just as the relative P/E gets interesting. Contrarian setups always look like this.
items.tweetB: Cheaper isn't cheap enough. Multiple compression with rising capex is not margin of safety.

items.title: SOX forward P/E back to AI-cycle low: 16x
items.idea: SOX fwd P/E fell to AI-cycle lows at just 16x forward earnings (GS/Bloomberg). The reset has been brutal; question is whether cheaper multiples attract buyers while momentum and credit stay ugly.
items.angle: Semis at 16x forward is a valuation not seen in the AI cycle. Estimates are the risk.
items.tweetA: 16x forward for semis is a number from before this cycle began. If the earnings hold, this is the chart of the year. If estimates fall, it's a value trap.
items.tweetB: Price is a lagging estimate of future earnings. At 16x the market is pricing capex digestion.

charts.desc: SOX forward P/E at AI-cycle low.

items.title: Oil long trap: trend followers entered the selloff heavily long energy
items.idea: CTAs entered Monday's selloff heavily long energy; with key technical levels under pressure, systematic sellers could drive a self-reinforcing liquidation.
items.angle: Mechanical unwind into a headline-driven drop. Energy CTA positioning is the amplifier.
items.tweetA: Trend followers were long energy into a 7% drop. The headline set the direction; their stop-losses set the magnitude.
items.tweetB: Peace-talk headline plus long CTA positioning equals overshoot risk. The level to watch is whether $96 WTI holds.

items.title: Oil vol trap: spec and macro accounts bought crude calls, 1y implied vol at 3-year high
items.idea: GS's Tallulah Adams: speculative and macro accounts were sizeable buyers of crude calls while implied vol surged; one-year vol hit three-year highs. Options priced escalating upside risk, a mismatch against Monday's price drop.
items.angle: Calls bought at peak vol into a -7% day: the pain trade for crowded long-vol energy.
items.tweetA: Calls bought, vol at 3-year highs, price down 7% in a day. That is the worst payoff profile in options: right direction thesis, wrong timing, max premium.
items.tweetB: Implied vol at a 3y high with oil falling: the market is still pricing escalation. A deal collapses that vol.

charts.desc: Crude implied vol and call buying (GS).

items.title: Beats are rewarded outside TMT (+1.72%) and punished inside (-0.76%)
items.idea: GS earnings work: companies beating EPS estimates outperform the S&P by a median 1.52pp the next day; within TMT the figure is -0.76%, outside TMT +1.72%. Lord Fed: good earnings are rewarded, just in different parts of the market. If not for AI names, the S&P would have been green in October.
items.angle: Rotation is real: reward for beats exists but not in the cohort that carries the index.
items.tweetA: Beat and gain 1.72% if you're not TMT. Beat and lose 0.76% if you are. The market is paying for earnings, just not in the stocks that own the index.
items.tweetB: S&P would have been green in October ex-AI. Equal-weight has been the actual market. The cap-weight index is a different instrument.

items.title: MSFT Azure +48% cc with 49-50% guide vs META operating cash $32.8B, capex $34.9B, FCF -$2.1B
items.idea: Lord Fed (long META and MSFT): Azure grew 48% constant currency, guide 49-50% next quarter, demand still exceeds supply; operating cash flow $58B, FCF $18.6B. META generated $32.8B operating cash but spent $34.9B capex, FCF -$2.1B. Frames the 'next-cheque problem': the market wants to know what shareholders get out of the spend.
items.angle: Demand answered, funding unanswered. The cleanest side-by-side of the hyperscaler cash-conversion split.
items.tweetA: Microsoft: $58B operating cash, $18.6B FCF. Meta: $32.8B operating cash, -$2.1B FCF. Same capex theme, opposite shareholder math. The market stopped lumping them together on Thursday.
items.tweetB: Azure +48% with demand above supply. The business is fine. The financing question isn't about demand, it's about who writes the next cheque. That's a credit question.

items.title: Thursday: 406 S&P names closed green, index closed red
items.idea: Lord Fed: broadening is still there; on Thursday 406 names were green yet the index finished red. A strong week for earnings turned into a poor week for his book as 'early breakout attempt' unraveled.
items.angle: Cap-weighted vs equal-weight divergence. Supports the Safe-is-expensive / rotation framework.
items.tweetA: 406 up, index down. The S&P is a 10-stock index with 490 passengers.
items.tweetB: Breadth is positive on up days for the median stock while the trend count (50/200) falls. Two breadth measures telling opposite stories. One of them is lagging.

items.title: 'Macro D' FX book approaching +60% YTD; 9 macro FX trades for November
items.idea: Paper Alfa's monthly Trade Corner: Macro D's YTD returns are approaching 60%, with 9 FX trades across DM and EM spanning diverging policy paths, relative rate advantages, shifting risk premia and valuation gaps. Body is a teaser — trades are paywalled.
items.angle: A discretionary macro FX book at +60% YTD is outlier performance; the 9 trades themselves are behind the paywall.
items.tweetA: A macro FX book up ~60% YTD, in a year when carry and policy divergence did most of the work. FX has been the quiet alpha market of 2026.
items.tweetB: The author says conviction must be earned, not borrowed from past performance. The line on risk-taking after a +60% year is worth more than the trade list.

items.title: Set up the trial, then ask for the money — Looker's hands-on trial playbook
items.idea: Looker founder Lloyd Tabb (First Round, April 2024): the team ran every free trial themselves — set up the software for the customer, taught them, watched them use it — and only then started the sales conversation. Self-serve trials fail because prospects log in, poke around, and never return.
items.angle: Founder-led onboarding as sales motion. Counter to PLG orthodoxy; relevant in AI products where setup is the barrier.
items.tweetA: Looker did white-glove trials before white-glove was a thing. In the AI era, 'we set it up for you' is the moat against the 10,000 copilots with a free tier.
items.tweetB: Free trial conversion fails on activation, not on price. Services-led onboarding is what the AI-agent startups are quietly rediscovering.

items.title: Bob Bowman on winning: build every plan backward from a 'dream goal'
items.idea: Phelps' coach Bob Bowman, in conversation with McKinsey senior partners, on how he defines winning, builds plans backward from a 'dream goal', and creates a culture where people want feedback. Anecdote: Phelps' goggles filled with water in the 2008 200m butterfly final; he counted strokes from practice and set a world record.
items.angle: Rehearsed-failure as performance system; relevant to risk process.
items.tweetA: Phelps swam a world record blind because he'd rehearsed failure. Most trading desks rehearse the win and improvise the loss.
items.tweetB: Backward-planning from a dream goal vs the usual 'process, not outcome' creed. Which one survives a drawdown?
